items.title: Saturday Posted & Toasted Notes: Wise men, French presidents, BrickBron James
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
Last weekend without basketball, fellas, so here’s a quick summary of a bunch of stuff that popped up recently around the NBA before we get down to (yeah, I know, , but still…) business.

  • James Wiseman has emerged as the early favorite for the Knicks’ 14th and likely final standard roster spot, according to the New York Post’s Stefan Bondy. Nothing new considering we’ve been talking about New York prioritizing a third center for months on end. In Bondy’s eyes, Tony Bradley and Drew Eubanks are Wiseman’s primary competition up front, while Bruce Brown and Ochai Agbaji are also fighting for the last spot in the Knicks’ roster.
  • Mike Brown, however, isn’t ready to declare Wiseman—or anybody else—the winner of that roster battle.

“I’m just going to let it unfold. I got no expectations. I’m not trying to forecast anything. I’m just taking this literally one practice at a time, one game at a time. And at the end of the day, when it comes time for us to figure out who’s going to be on the final roster, we’ll do it.”

  • The Athletic’s James L. Edwards III identified whether the Knicks can maintain their edge after winning the championship as New York’s biggest question entering the new season.
  • In another piece published over The Athletic, multiple reporters assembled three perspectives on the Knicks’ chances of repeating, and none were especially bullish.
  • Anne Hathaway would sacrifice another Oscar for another Knicks championship.
  • The Pistons and Jalen Duren finally found common ground, with the big boy and postseason no-shower inking a five-year, $200 million deal… without a weight clause on it.
  • Victor Wembanyama hasn’t even won an NBA title, but he’s already thinking about running for President of France.
  • It looks like the Las Vegas Whatevers are a very real thing and will get a franchise approved before Seattle does, but that could come with the con of having to wait an extra year to enter NBA play, contrary to the SuperSonics 2.0 making their comeback in time for the 2028-29 campaign.
  • JaVale McGee has joined the Shanghai Sharks, teaming up with D’Angelo Russell in China. Yes, that’s a real headline.
  • LeBron stans are already aboard the #lbjmvp train. Meanwhile…

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘Either joint replacement, let it go, or, I guess, amputation’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
My brain melted yesterday, thought it was Sunday, not Thursday.

Anyway, today’s Friday. I guess.

Here’s the latest from Tarrytown as we keep hearing from different Knicks.

On Josh Hart’s injured finger and the toughness it reflects:

“Josh, he’s a handsome young man. But that finger is ugly. So, I don’t look at it. But it adds to his toughness. Josh is a tough son of a gun, man. I can’t even watch when he [shakes his hand], because I’m just like, oh, my gosh I can’t imagine having a finger like that.

“But it just shows who he is. He’s tough but, more importantly, there’s dedication there to wanting to be a great shooter, and you’ve got to put it into work. And he puts in the work, even though his finger’s bothering him. And even though it’s a little crooked, he’s putting in the work to get it right. [Shooting coach] Pete [Patton] and the rest of the coaches are helping him out, and it shows that he can shoot at a high level with the dedication he has in the first place.”

On OG Anunoby’s playoff performance boosting his All-Star case:

“It should help him a ton because guys that are quiet naturally, they have a hard time getting the necessary publicity and promotion toward being an All-Star, unless you’re doing something extraordinary and people start talking about it — like OG in the playoffs. So doing it in the playoffs and having people talk about it should have carryover, in my opinion, since he helped us win the championship.

“And he was in the conversation for [NBA] Finals MVP. That should definitely help create calls for him to have a case to be an All-Star this year. He’s still got to go earn it, but he should be in everybody’s conversation from the beginning.”

On Anunoby’s shooting ability:

“He’s not [at Stephen Curry] or [Klay Thompson’s] level but the next tier. He’s way better than I thought.”

On Anunoby’s confidence, shooting and the Knicks’ spacing:

“His confidence is really high. And I thought during the playoffs we did a really good job of touching the paint and taking the right 3s. With OG being 6-foot-7 with long arms, if you’re closing to him with a smaller guy or a guard, it’s going to be good for us because they try to put their best player on Jalen, and sometimes, their best player is a bigger perimeter defender.

“So that means OG may have a smaller guy [defending him]. That’s not impacting him when he shoots the basketball.

“So I think first starts off with him, yes; he’s way better than what I thought. I would categorize him as a great shooter. But more importantly, I thought our spacing and our ability to touch the paint and spray it helped out a lot.”

On his plans for the preseason games:

“We’ll try to ease them in. The last game is always a dress rehearsal, but we’ll try to build them up leading to that game.”

On the Knicks’ conditioning entering camp after a short summer:

“All the guys look like they’re in pretty good shape, especially for a short summer. We have a conditioning test that we did last year and this year that the guys have to pass to get into camp and they all passed it.”

On James Wiseman’s presence at training camp:

“Fantastic human being, fantastic young man…. Good to see him in the gym. When you’re that long and that athletic, with skill – he has skill – there’s a place for you in this league. Sometimes it takes the right moment, the right team, the right situation, all that stuff, to be able to fit someplace and grow. We have a lot of great guys in camp that have potential of impacting us in a lot of different ways throughout the course of the year. He’s definitely one of the many guys that we have that we’re excited about.”

On Tony Bradley after his training camp signing:

“We’re looking for bigs. Tony’s a veteran guy that’s still in his prime and has a good feel for the game, knows how to play the game the right way and he’s hurt us in the past. To be honest, when a guy hurts you in the past, you tend to remember him more than others. So to be able to add him to camp was a positive for us because again, I said this last year, (Karl-Anthony Towns) has one of the most (challenging positions) out of everybody because I want to move him around when I play him at center. I want to play him at power forward; (when he’s at) power forward 1-4 is interchangeable. Same with OG (Anunoby). OG we put him at the 5 last year. We probably will do it a little bit more this year as well.

“But to be able to do that, you’ve gotta have enough centers around on the team, so having Tony here with his skill set and feel is definitely a blessing because we’re looking at that position heavily.”

On the options to fix his finger:

“The only option for my finger at this point, because of how damaged it is, is a full joint replacement. With a joint replacement, you can’t have the banging, grabbing a rebound, palming it, shooting, catching the ball, doing all that. You can’t do that. So if I did a joint replacement, then I wouldn’t be able to play. So I guess it’s either wrap it until I retire or cut it off. I guess that’s the other option. That’s really the only alternative: either joint replacement, let it go, or, I guess, amputation.

“I mean, there was a lot of stuff that I had to get checked, and that was one of them. It was just with how it deteriorated, the joint and the bone and everything, that’s what it’ll be. So I’ll do that probably when I retire. Hopefully, they can make it straight. You know, it’s a little off center if y’all didn’t realize. So I’m hoping after that joint replacement it can kind of get a little straighter.”

On how the pain in his finger varies from day to day:

“Some days, it’ll be good. Some days it’ll hurt to catch the ball. It varies. I wish I could tell you when I wake up what’s gonna be good, what’s gonna be bad. Somedays it’s good, like a regular functioning finger. And other days it hurts to just close my hand, to make a fist.”

On why a joint replacement would prevent him from playing basketball:

“You can’t have the banging, you know, repetitive, grabbing a rebound, palming it, shooting, catching the ball, doing all that; you can’t do that. It was just with how it deteriorated — the joint and the bone and everything — that’s what it’ll be. So I’ll do that probably when I retire. Hopefully they can make it straight. You know, it’s a little off center if you know y’all didn’t realize.”

On the appearance and functionality of his injured finger:

“I mean, it’s it’s not the prettiest to look at. I would love to have a straight finger, but you know, it works.”

On the physical toll of an NBA career and what fans don’t get:

“I think people think money is everything, and for me, obviously, you want to be compensated fairly for your performance and all that. But at the end of the day, just because you get paid, be blessed in a position to get paid well and take care of our families, [it’s not like] we’re not humans at the same time. I’m sitting here thinking, my knees are aching a little bit, but I want to leave the game and be able to run around and play with my kids when they’re you know 10, 11,12-plus. So that wear and tear, it’s significant to a certain point. If you’re in this league for 14, 15, 16 years, and you see some of these guys that are older, they they got limps, knees are barking, those kind of things. So I think that definitely gets overlooked. But that’s also why I don’t think I’ll play till I’m 40.”

On OG Anunoby’s increased recognition helping his All-Star chances:

“It’s extremely impactful. Obviously, you have to be a gifted and good player to make an All-Star team, but also you have to have the press and all that kind of behind you, bolstering it. So it’s good for people to see how talented he is, how impactful he is on both sides of the ball in the game. So hopefully that recognition will continue throughout this year, and hopefully we’ll be able to get him in.”

On Jalen Brunson’s increased fame following the Knicks title:

“He’s not LeBron, let’s relax.”

On planning to attend Yankees Game 3:

“I think I’m going to be able to get to Game 3. We have a preseason game the next day. So I’m excited, man. I’m excited for New York. Excited for that team.”

On OG Anunoby’s playoff success boosting his confidence:

“That’s definitely a boost of confidence going into this year. OG knows how good he is, and we know how good he is. So he’s gonna continue doing what he does.”

On learning the backcourt rule during his late Game 4 possession:

“I learned on the fly. When I watched the video after, they said you can leave the ball in the backcourt but your body can be in the frontcourt – I didn’t know it was a thing until then. I’m glad it worked out.”

On what has allowed the Knicks to embrace their roles:

“We care for each other, we compete, we want to get each other better”

On whether he always planned to return to the Knicks before signing his extension:

“In my mind, yeah. ‘I want to stay here, I want to stay home.’ We had a chance to do that, and we did it.”

On his championship summer:

“My favorite summer of all time”

items.title: On This Date in Knicks History: October 2
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
Two noteworthy Knicks birthdays today!

Dr. Dick Barnett was born October 2, 1936, in Gary, Indiana. Barnett spent eight seasons with New York, became an All-Star in 1968, and played for both the 1970 and 1973 championship teams. His number 12 hangs in the Garden rafters. He died last year at 88.

Barnett had one of the most unforgettable shots in basketball history. Starting in college (when nicknamed “Dick the Skull”), he became known for contorting his body into a question mark while shooting his jumper, kicking his legs back and telling defenders, “Too late–fall back, baby!” Barnett went on to turn his eccentric shot into more than 15,000 NBA points.

A beloved teammate of Walt Frazier, Barnett was featured in the documentary film, , about his time playing at Tennessee State University for the Tigers. During segregation, the all-Black Tigers won three straight national championships. Captain Barnett tirelessly fought for their recognition, which culminated in their 2019 induction into the Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame. Watch the doc here, you’ll dig it.

After hanging up his sneakers, Barnett earned an MBA from New York University and then a PhD in education from Fordham University. He taught Sports Management at St. John’s University for four years.

  • 2× NBA champion (1970, 1973)
  • All-ABL First Team (1962)
  • No. 12 retired by New York Knicks
  • 3× NAIA champion (1957–1959)
  • 3× AP Little College All-American (1957–1959)
  • 2× UPI Little College All-American (1958, 1959)
  • 2× NAIA tournament MVP (1958, 1959)

And (feeling like Garrison Keillor here) Tyson Chandler was born today in 1982, in Hanford, California. Chandler came to New York immediately after anchoring Dallas’ 2011 championship defense and became the 2011-12 NBA Defensive Player of the Year, the only Knick ever to take the honor.

Drafted second in 2001, the seven-foot Chandler played for five seasons in Chicago before bouncing from NOLA to Charlotte to Dallas and then the Knicks. After three seasons at MSG, he was sent back to Dallas, then Phoenix, and finished out his 19-year career with the Lakers and Rockets.

Chandler joined the Knicks in December 2011 via a sign-and-trade between multiple teams, which also sent traded Ronny Turiaf, cash, and a 2013 2nd-round draft pick to the Wizards. While there was no denying his talent, Chandler appeared on the injured list often during his tenure here, with a hamstring strain, playoff flu and an upper respiratory infection, a bulging cervical disc (plus related neck spasms and weight loss from illness), and a fractured right fibula.

In June 2014, he and Raymond Felton were traded to the Mavs for José Calderón, Samuel Dalembert, Wayne Ellington, Shane Larkin, a 2014 2nd-round draft pick (Thanasis Antetokounmpo was later selected), and a 2014 2nd-round draft pick (Cleanthony Early was later selected). (h/t basketball-reference.com)

Chandler concluded his time in New York with averages of 10.2 points, 10.1 rebounds, and 1.2 blocks across 183 games. His career highlights, also from Wikipedia:

  • All-NBA Third Team (2012)
  • NBA Defensive Player of the Year (2012)
  • NBA All-Defensive First Team (2013)
  • 2× NBA All-Defensive Second Team (2011, 2012)
  • First-team Parade All-American (2001)
  • Second-team Parade All-American (2000)
  • McDonald’s All-American (2001)
  • 2× California Mr. Basketball (2000, 2001)

Quite a nice pairing: two Knicks born 46 years apart, one remembered for his offense, the other for defense. Closing my Writer’s Almanac loop, your poem for the day is a personal favorite, “The Bear,” by Galway Kinnell.

Knicks in five. And keep in touch.

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘I’ll let the front office and my agency handle that’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
Would you believe the Knicks play basketball next week!?

That’s right, and they do so against the Philadelphia 76ers of all teams, one that surely pays homage to the age of their roster with their moniker.

Here’s the latest we heard straight out of Tarrytown and elsewhere on Wednesday.

On eventually discussing Miles McBride’s contract situation with him:

“There will probably be a time and place where I talk to him about that because he’s human, and we all want what’s best for ourselves, our families, as well as the organization. That’s a nice balancing act, but at the end of the day, he wants to be here, we want him to be here, and that’s something that I have faith in Leon and Deuce’s representatives to figure that out.”

On staying out of the Knicks’ contract negotiations:

“It literally is the [salary] cap’s above my head. I don’t know how that works, and we’ve got a lot of moving parts as we all know. So I’m gonna let that unfold how it unfolds and in the meantime, we’re all just worried about how we can help each other on the court more than anything else because we know off the court, things get taken care of the right way here.”

On Gregg Popovich reaching out during the Knicks’ playoff run:

“[Pop] is grizzled, experienced. He understands how this works. We actually talked a couple of times during the playoffs. After OG’s tip-in, he called me and talked me through a lot of things. It was great to have conversations with him from time to time.”

On the support he received from the NBA coaching community after winning the championship:

“The coaching community is tight. Everybody wants everybody to do well because they know that the guy across from them is the one that really knows what I’m going through or the other guy’s going through. So because it’s that hard we really try to uplift one another whenever we can and when we won it, a lot of guys reached out if not everybody, and said congratulations in some way shape or form. It was great.”

On the Knicks looking for more centers:

“We’re looking for bigs. We’re looking at that [center] position heavily.”

On adding Tony Bradley and the need for center depth:

“Tony’s a veteran guy that’s still in his prime and has a good feel for the game, knows how to play the game the right way and he’s hurt us in the past. And, to be honest, when a guy hurts you in the past, you tend to remember him more than others. So to be able to add him to camp was a positive for us because, again, I said this last year: KAT has one of the most [difficult] spots out of everybody because I want to move him around when I play him at center. I want to play him at power forward, and at power forward, one through four is interchangeable.

“Same with OG [Anunoby]. OG we put him at the 5 last year. We probably will do it a little bit more this year as well. But to be able to do that, you’ve gotta have enough centers around on the team, so having Tony here with his skill set and feel is definitely a blessing because we’re looking at that position heavily.”

On planning to use Karl-Anthony Towns and OG at multiple positions:

“I want to play him at center, I want to play him at power forward.

“OG, we threw him at the five some last year. We probably will do a little bit more this year as well.”

On Josh Hart suddenly embracing the power forward label for the conditioning test:

“Josh was a power forward but when it came to the conditioning test, the power forwards and centers have an easier time [requirement]. Not much, but an easier time than guards. So all year I was calling him a power forward and he was cool with it but I could tell he didn’t really like it. But as soon as he heard about the conditioning test, he said he was a power forward.”

On wanting to remain with the Knicks for the rest of his career:

“Obviously, I love being in New York. I’d love to continue my career here, end my career here. Best fans, feel like we’ve done, obviously, something great this past year, and the years leading up to that. And I want to continue with this team.

“I’ve addressed a little bit earlier with some comments. But I’ll let the front office and my agency handle that.”

On being disappointed by the lack of a contract extension while remaining professional:

“It’s a little hard at times, but I’m gonna be a professional. I want to go out and do my job. So that’s in my ability, and to help the team win for as long as I’m with the team.”

On not allowing his contract uncertainty to affect his play:

“In a sense, every year you have to prove yourself. I feel like there’s uncertainty across the board for everybody in the league. Everybody’s going for big contracts and this and that. So I don’t let it really bother me. At the end of the day, I just want to go out there and give it my shot, play my best basketball.”

On whether he sees similarities in Mitchell Robinson’s departure and his situation:

“No, no. I mean, at the end of the day, it’s a business.”

On being fully healthy after recovering over the summer:

“I’m feeling a lot better. It’s kind of crazy thinking about how unhealthy I was playing through that playoff run. You go through surgery in an area where you need it. The easy medical term is sports hernia but it was a lot more complex than that. So having a summer under me, getting back fully healthy, it’s been so much better being able to move around how I want to move.

“They took my hip flexor, my abdomen and my groin and they pulled it and they put it in my pelvis and they did it on both sides. So trying to open a door, reach for a remote and everything you do is in that core, in that core section.

“So trying to keep up with those young guys in the Finals was tough.”

On the Knicks moving on from their championship summer:

“The summer that you’re champions, obviously, you only get to experience that for the summer, and then you’re right back to playing. I feel like we all had a good time. Everybody did the right thing over the summer. And we got right back to work when it was time to get back to work.”

On the Knicks’ championship bringing estranged families back together:

“I have people coming to me and saying, ‘I haven’t talked to my family member in 10 years,’ and I’m like, ‘Well, we should not be the reason that’s happening.’ But, you know, that’s cool to hear. Like I said, it’s not what I want to hear, necessarily, but those are cool moments to hear that what we’re doing on the court was able to bring people back together.”

On getting to take the Larry O’Brien Trophy to his high school:

“So you actually get to request it. You have to get approval from the front office and somebody in the front office is supposed to have it that weekend. They kindly let me have it, so shout out to Leon [Rose] for that. He let me have it for that weekend.”

On the security of his new Knicks contract:

“It definitely gives you a sense of perspective and appreciation that I’m grateful for. To be believed in and have that offered to me, for me and [his fiancée] Cammi to be able to stay here in New York and continue to grow this thing, it’s pretty special. To be asked to be a part of it is humbling and I’m grateful for it every day. It means a lot.”

On feeling proud after earning long-term security with the Knicks:

“In a way, it just makes me proud of myself. That’s why you work through the difficult times and the challenging and the questioning ones. Typically, there’s really good stuff on the other end of that. It feels good, it feels good to be a part of this moving forward. I don’t want to drop my level or get complacent or any of that, that’s definitely not the feeling. It’s more, it just feels good to know that you don’t have that heavy wave right on your ass again this training camp.”

On whether he has rewatched his Eastern Conference Finals 11-of-12-from-three performance:

“I haven’t watched it all back in full, no. I’ve seen little clips.”

On staying ready for his playoff opportunity:

“Playoffs are funny in that way, and I feel like I’ve been privy to that with my past experiences, where you sit and you’re not in the rotation, but you’re one or two games away from being called on, being relied on to do something. I don’t know, I kind of just had a feeling, I’ve seen this movie before. It worked out.”

On what his new contract means after years of uncertainty:

“Last couple of years I’ve been pretty open with you guys. It definitely gives you a sense of perspective and appreciation that I’m grateful for. To be believed in and have that offered to me, for me and Cammi to be able to stay here in New York and continue to grow this thing, it’s pretty special. To be asked to be a part of it is humbling and I’m grateful for it every day. It means a lot.”

On bringing the Larry O’Brien Trophy to his wedding:

“I took it on a date. I took it to my wedding. I asked to have it. I couldn’t have a wedding without Larry there, you know?”

On traveling with the trophy and still being amazed by winning it:

“He had a rider and all, and we made sure we got him there first class, and we got it done. So, I spent some time with the trophy this summer, and every time I see the trophy, I still can’t believe it.”

On being happy for his former Knicks teammates after their championship:

“I’m happy [for the Knicks], man. I kept in touch with guys. I’ve had a lot of great moments here in the city. I spent five years here, my family has grown here; so I was extremely excited, happy for those guys. A lot went into that; it’s not just myself, years before me.

“So, just happy for those guys. I was just last month on a trip with OG [Anunoby] in Brazil, just kicking it, talking with each other. So it was a great thing, not just for them, for the organization, [but] for the city that has craved that — we know how New York is — so has craved that winning formula, winning environment. And we plan to do the same thing here.”

On what Knicks and Yankees championships in the same year would mean:

“A Knicks championship in June and a Yankees World Series in October would bring world peace.”

On the Knicks’ championship run and his faith in the Yankees:

“It’s tough to go up against world champs like the Knicks, and the run they went on, it was so incredible with the ups and downs. But I got a lot of faith in these guys, man. We’ve got a special group here with a lot of grit.”

On the Yankees drawing inspiration from the Knicks:

“We’re definitely inspired by the Knicks, and we’ve got to keep the winning going in New York.”

On wanting the Yankees to create the same excitement in New York as the Knicks:

“Oh yeah, for sure, I can’t wait. I can’t wait until we go on that run. That’s what I want. I want the city to be on fire.

“It was amazing for me, especially for having friends on the (Knicks) team and being around them while it was going on. It was sick to watch.”

items.title: Thursday Posted & Toasted Notes: Candid KAT, roster math, criminal files
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
You don’t know how much I missed #KnicksSZN. Actually, if you’re reading this… I mean, you probably know as well.

Here’s the latest from Tarrytown and other NBA-related places.

  • Karl-Anthony Towns opened up extensively about what finally becoming an NBA champion meant after years of criticism. In an interview with The Athletic, he also detailed how during the Knicks’ miserable 2-9 January stretch and amid Giannis Antetokounmpo trade rumors, he and Jordyn Woods were apparently checking Milwaukee real estate.

“We were on Zillow looking at Milwaukee. Like, ‘Hey, babe, I went around town, and it’s not that bad. This could be a good spot right here.’”

  • Towns’ extension remains a significant unresolved issue, and ESPN’s Malika Andrews reported KAT is willing to take a discount similar in spirit to Brunson’s sacrifice… but “the pay cut that the Knicks are asking him to take, he views as unreasonable.” Uh, oh.
  • Isiah Thomas is returning to the organization, folks. He’ll be part of the NYK board of directors. The move is part of the recently confirmed MSG split of the Rangers and the Knicks.
  • The Knicks still haven’t decided whether they will make the traditional championship visit to the White House despite James Dolan saying in June that the organization had accepted an invitation.
  • Bobby Marks’ Knicks training-camp snapshot for ESPN underscores how tight the roster math is, with the pundit watching “the frontcourt and final roster spots” as the key remaining thing to solve before New York kicks off its title-defense season.
  • Former Knicks guard J.R. Smith was arrested in Texas on a charge of assault causing bodily injury-family violence after police said a traffic stop revealed an active warrant from the Southlake Police Department.
  • Phoenix Suns villain Dillon Brooks has been charged with driving under the influence, per TMZ. Being arrested is a trend these days.
  • About LeBron’s Philadelphia era, James is indeed splitting his time between New York City and Philadelphia and commuting by helicopter.
  • The NBA is reportedly gaining momentum toward agreements with major European soccer clubs for its planned NBA Europe competition, which is targeted to launch next fall.
  • OAKAAK Carmelo Anthony knows very clearly what he’d do with Jalen Duren if he were in charge of the Pistons’ operations.
  • Shortly after the Grizzlies released D’Angelo Russell, the mighty point guard and former No. 2 overall pick from the 2015 NBA draft is flying to China to play for the Shanghai Sharks, and joining an illustrious list of NBA alumni to play for the organization.
  • Tyler Herro was traded from the Heat to the Bucks, but he’s happy to leave the “Capital of Distraction” for… a place somewhere in Wisconsin?
  • Former Knicks’ first-round pick Kristaps Porzingis won’t be able to participate in the Warriors’ training camp due to an undisclosed “health issue.” Somebody give this man a break.
  • Nikola Jokic isn’t close to turning his full attention to horses.
  • The New York Liberty just became the first-ever No. 8 seed to send the No. 1 seed (Minnesota Lynx) home in the WNBA playoffs. Now, let’s finish this business.

items.title: Dumping Deuce Not Advised
items.author: John Gove
items.content:
Seasoned Knicks fans have doctorate degrees in roster construction, with a primary focus on asset management. For over a decade, we spent countless hours discussing expiring contracts, tracking picks, and praying the day would come when all the “futures thinking” translated into a legitimate championship window.

Well, we made it. Like the driver-side door on my red Nissan Rogue, the window is now open. But now that repeating as champions is the goal, New York’s roster-building approach is shifting again. That shift directly brings our focus to Miles “Deuce” McBride and his future with the Knicks.

Entering the final year of his contract, it is no secret that talks between Deuce and the Knicks have stalled. All signs point to him wanting to stay in New York. The fan base would love him to remain as a key piece of the rotation. However, ownership and the front office are fretting about wearing two aprons while making their prize-winning pizza, especially with Jim Dolan looking over their shoulders.

Because of that fearful culinary attire (too many second-apron jokes?), a growing segment of the fanbase is convinced the Knicks must flip him before the trade deadline. Whether it’s to recoup a draft pick or fill a worrisome hole at center, Deuce cannot simply walk away for nothing. OK, sure he can. And maybe he does. Regardless, trading him away because of that worry would be a majorly short-sighted mistake.

New York finds itself in a bit of a financial gridlock. After sacrificing about $113M to help the team, Brunson will be extension eligible next summer (). Anunoby and Bridges are secure for now (on ascending contracts), Hart would like to extend now, and throw in a monster contract for Towns, and there’s not much wiggle room.

In the old NBA, James Dolan could scribble out a luxury-tax check to keep a fan favorite around. Then the 2023 CBA introduced a first apron (roughly $8–9M above the tax line) and a second apron (roughly $17–21M+ above the tax line, depending on the year; e.g., ~$221.7M for 2026-27). Crossing that damned second apron doesn’t just trigger a tax penalty; it hijacks a team’s roster-building. If you cross the line, you lose trade flexibility, the ability to aggregate salaries, and future first-round picks get frozen like Jack Dawson at the end of .

Unfortunately, Deuce is a potential casualty of math. He’ll undoubtedly earn a significant pay raise in his next contract. However, the Knicks can’t give him one without dismantling a starting five that just brought New York a championship… and appeared on Saturday Night Live. He isn’t a financial priority because the money could be spent more intelligently elsewhere. That’s just the reality of the business.

So, if the Knicks probably cannot pay the guy, why not trade him now? Well, that answer has two parts. First, what he does on the court can’t be easily replaced. Second, he gets paid very little (relatively speaking) to do it.

Deuce is making a “meager” $3.96 million this season. That kind of contract is a cheat code for a contending team. In the trade market, however, it is a major limitation. An outgoing $4 million salary doesn’t bring back a game-changing asset.

Consider how Deuce’s skill set impacts New York’s production on both ends of the court. Averaging 12 points per game last year and shooting roughly 40% from three, he spaces the floor well with Brunson and punishes defenses that try to double the captain. Defensively, he is relentless at the point of attack. He picks up opposing guards full court, navigates ball screens, and takes on the most tiresome defensive assignment to give the primary producers a break. You cannot find that level of two-way reliability for under $4 million.

But John… We desperately need a center!

I mean, you’re not entirely wrong. Big Mitch is gone and glancing at the center depth chart is enough to raise anyone’s blood pressure. Looking at Deuce as the best trade chip is tempting and convincing yourself we can flip him for a big man is quite easy to do.

But trading an elite rotational guard for a stopgap center that potentially might not play a whole lot is terrible roster management. Do the math for a minute. If we trade Deuce’s contract, we have to bring back a $4 million center. That gets the Knicks a deepl flawed, third-string big man destined to get hunted in the pick-and-roll and become nonexistent come playoff time. Anyone willing to trade a guy who plays closing minutes in crucial games for a big who will consistently rock the warmup gear should not be employed by an NBA front office.

New York can survive the early schedule by signing a low-cost option and patch the center rotation by committee, and even have OG play a little five (as Mike Brown even mentioned.) It gives them time to evaluate the landscape and see what shakes out throughout the league. Panicking in October and trading our best bench piece does nothing but hurts the organization’s title odds.

There is also precedent to consider. The Knicks brass were probably well-aware that they would not be able to afford to re-sign Mitchell Robinson this summer—and his departure is the reason why we’re in this pickle at center. Leon Rose must have heard some interest in Mitch before the in-season trade deadline, but he held on to the asset. Unless there’s a – we suspect he’ll do the same with Deuce.

Forward-thinking got the Knicks where they are today. Focussing on the present is how they hang another championship banner up in Madison Square Garden for the second straight year.

Letting a talented, 26-year-old guard hit unrestricted free agency without getting anything in return goes against everything we have been conditioned to believe. It might sting a little but the ultimate goal of asset management isn’t to pretty up the perfect spreadsheet. It is to win a championship. Miles McBride helps this roster win games this season.

If we have to accept the 2026-27 campaign is essentially a one-year, rental of Deuce, so be it. Keep him on the roster! Let him lock down the opposition and hit clutch threes for us as we look for two in a row. If another franchise throws $20 million at him next summer, we simply song that catchy Fall Out Boy song and tell the man, “Thanks for the memories.”

The window for winning is right now. You don’t close it early just to save a few bucks and appease the armchair analysts.

items.title: Knicks enter camp looking to perfect their championship offense
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
You hear versions of the story often. Here’s one that might be apocryphal (forgive me if I get it wrong; I’m bottle-feeding a rescued kitten every two hours and haven’t slept properly since Friday). Rock juggernaut Def Leppard was almost finished recording their follow-up to the multi-platinum , and their track list was locked down when producer Mutt Lange heard singer Joe Elliott strumming something new during a break. Mutt deemed this song a worthy, eleventh-hour addition to the album. That little ditty? “Pour Some Sugar on Me.” Huge hit. Ask your parents.

Sometimes a late change, whether accidental or desperate, can alter the fates. In April 2026, the third-seeded New York Knickerbockers found themselves trailing the sixth-seeded Atlanta Hawks two games to one. Our heroes had spent months stress-testing their systems and preparing for a deep playoff run only to get cut up by the honorable, but aging, CJ McCollum.

With their backs against the proverbial wall, coach Mike Brown recognized the need for a change. His central adjustment placed Karl-Anthony Towns in a facilitating role farther out from the basket. This reduced the creation load on Jalen Brunson, highlighted Towns’ vision as a passer, drew opposing bigs away from the rim, and created opportunities for the wings to cut and screen effectively.

New York’s overall scoring efficiency rose sharply, posting an offensive rating near 124 points per 100 possessions and a record-shattering point differential. Operating in high gear, they went on a 15-1 run that delivered them to the promised land. And there was great rejoicing.

Training camp for the 2026-27 season began this week. Now Coach Brown has a chance to refine and expand on his winning formula.

Early reports from training camp indicate that Towns’ hub role will remain a priority, as the coaching staff plans to increase elbow involvement for KAT and explore additional ways to involve the wings across the floor. Their options include testing new Knick Andre Drummond as a secondary facilitator and giving OG Anunoby more minutes at center. During the playoffs, OG in particular produced some of his strongest stretches by generating offense off the bounce. Moving him into a small-ball center role with more interior and mid-floor actions could help maximize his impact, especially with limited traditional center depth behind Towns.

(Unrelated: OG needs a nickname on his Basketball-Reference page. Help us out.)

Coach Brown used the first day of camp to temper expectations that might/can/probably should arise from New York’s legendary postseason finish. He said the regular season will inevitably include adversity and periods when the team does not resemble its postseason peak. Mike has an entire training camp to formalize something that succeeded partly because opponents had little time to prepare for it. Now they know what’s coming. To repeat their championship, the veteran skipper might need a new ace up his sleeve for the next postseason.

Maybe that’s why Rajon Rondo appeared at the practice facility this week. Brunson has formed a connection with the two-time champion in recent months and described the former Celtics point guard as a player he watched growing up. As for what he admired, Jalen specifically cited Rondo’s creativity and unusual way of seeing the game.

New York may need to explore some fresh ideas if they intend to remain atop the mountain. Sustaining success is difficult in any field, as Def Leppard found out. Almost 40 years later, “Pour Some Sugar on Me” remains their biggest hit. We waited five decades for a championship. We’d rather not wait so long for the next one.

items.title: Knicks sign Tony Bradley and Jaden Akins in training camp roster shakeup
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
The Knicks are not quite done sorting out their training camp roster.

On Wednesday morning, as we creep ever closer to next Monday’s preseason opener, the Knicks made a series of roster moves at the back of their training camp roster:

  • Waived John Konchar and N’Faly Dante
  • Signed Tony Bradley to an Exhibit 9 contract
  • Signed Jaden Akins to a two-way contract

There’s a few layers to unpack here, so let’s start with the two new Knicks.

You may remember Bradley from his reserve-center minutes for the Indiana Pacers and Atlanta Hawks in the last two postseasons. Picked No. 28 overall by the Lakers in the 2017 draft out of UNC, Bradley will look to make the roster of his seventh team. He started his career as a seldom-used backup big for the Jazz, playing just 12 games total in his first two seasons. He upgraded to being a solid bench player in 2019-20, but then became a complete journeyman.

He was traded twice in one week before the 2020-21 season, from Utah to Detroit to Philadelphia, before being shipped out again in March 2021 to the Thunder in a three-team deal that involved the Knicks (the Austin Rivers trade, if you recall). He balled out in 20 games down the stretch, averaging 8.7 points and 6.1 rebounds, the best stretch of his career. After playing 55 games for the Bulls in 2021-22, he hasn’t played more than 41 in a season since.

He joined the Pacers in 2024 and was their third center on their run to the NBA Finals, playing 38 minutes total in the Eastern Conference Finals against the Knicks, being a plus-15 in fairly minor action.

Bradley found his way to Atlanta midway through the 2025-26 season and played four games in that first-round series too, most notably being minus-17 in the Game 5 blowout.

He has a few interesting links to the Knicks aside from the playoffs. He was traded by the Lakers on draft night to Utah for… Josh Hart and Thomas Bryant. When he was sent to Philly in November 2020, it was in a 1-for-1 deal with lottery bust Zhaire Smith, whom the Sixers infamously chose over Mikal Bridges. In that three-team swap in 2021, he was traded with the second-round pick that became Tyler Nickel… to OKC.

As for Akins, he’s getting his first NBA opportunity. The former All-Big Ten guard went undrafted out of Michigan State in 2025 and spent the 2025-26 season with the Motor City Cruise, the G League affiliate of the Pistons, where he averaged 14.7 points and 4.4 assists on 41.2% from the field and 35.8% from three.

The 23-year-old was with the Knicks in Summer League this year, averaging 11.3 points a night. He was already ticketed for Westchester after signing an Exhibit 10 earlier this month before being subsequently waived, but the Knicks elected to fill their final two-way spot with a guy who’s already in-house.

The other two moves could turn out to be just procedural, or could be the sign of the organization going in a different direction.

Konchar, the former Grizzlies wing, did not report to training camp with the rest of the roster due to personal reasons. Ian Begley said the motivation for waiving him was to give him more time to deal with his situation, leaving the door open for a potential return down the road. The fact that he said that makes me believe the org thinks highly of him and had him towards the top for consideration for a roster spot.

Dante, the former Oregon Duck and brief Hawk and Rocket, was also waived. He is recovering from a torn ACL, and it isn’t surprising if the team deems him more G League fodder, but I found it interesting that he was posted as part of Media Day coverage on Monday. Not sure they’d do that with a guy they had no plans for, so maybe they’ll stash him in Westchester and consider him for a two-way when he’s healthy.

Here’s the updated training camp roster:

Jalen Brunson, Josh Hart, Mikal Bridges, OG Anunoby, Karl-Anthony Towns, Deuce McBride, Jose Alvarado, Landry Shamet, Andre Drummond, Jordan Clarkson, Tyler Kolek, Pacome Dadiet, Mo Diawara

Drew Eubanks, Bruce Brown, Ochai Agbaji, James Wiseman, Tony Bradley

Tyler Nickel, Kevin McCullar Jr., Jaden Akins

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘If I get a joint replacement, my career is over’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
Can you feel it in the air? It’s Knicks basketball scent.

New York keeps working through the early days of training camp, gearing up for a preseason matchup with the 76ers on Oct. 5.

Meanwhile, here’s the latest we’ve heard about the Knickerbockers inside the Tarrytown facilities and elsewhere.

On Andre Drummond being quicker and more explosive than expected:

“He’s a little quicker and more explosive.”

On Andre Drummond replacing Mitchell Robinson by being himself:

“We’re not expecting Andre to come in and be Mitch or impact the game in a lot of different ways that Mitch did. Just be yourself, but everyone else has to step up and box-out a little harder. All those things will make us a top-level team.”

On Drummond’s veteran experience, instincts and mobility:

“He’s a veteran. He’s been there, done that with a few different teams, and he’s a big body, he’s got great feet. Seems like his instincts are pretty good on both ends of the floor. His feet are quicker than what you could imagine. He’s really light on his feet, which is a good thing.”

On the Knicks still discussing a potential White House visit:

“No, that’s still something that our guys, the organization, is internally discussing. Whatever we decide to do we’ll all do together.”

On his expectations for the Knicksover the 82-game regular season:

“We’re not playing at that level for 82 games. You know, we played at a pretty high level, and … that’s not going to happen over 82 games. You know, for me, the 82-game season is about trying to find your way.”

On expanding the Knicks’ offense around Karl-Anthony Towns and experimenting with different lineups:

“Obviously playing with KAT at the elbow a little bit more than what we did [in the regular season last year]. Being with this group for a year now, you get a better feel of what players can do what. Like I didn’t know if OG could be as effective as he was in the pick-and-roll game. Same with Mikal. So to try to continue to find ways to get those guys involved at the top of the floor is something that we’ll take a look at.

“We have great cutters that have tremendous size. We’ll continue to mix that in, and we all know that KAT is a really good facilitator at the elbow. Maybe Andre [Drummond] is too? I don’t know. Maybe we move OG to the five a little bit more than what we did last year. So there are a lot of different ways we can go with the team on both ends of the floor. The biggest thing is knowing that nothing’s set in stone.”

On carrying over the Knicks’ playoff offense into the new season while continuing to evolve:

“There’s a lot that will carry over for this year. We’ll also experiment with some new things here and there, but the stuff that we had in the playoffs may not work during the regular season. So we have to be ready to evolve or pivot as the year goes along and hopefully come close to playoff time, we’re trending upwards so that we feel we’re in a pretty good spot with the confidence needed to take off from there.”

On Andre Drummond’s potential importance to the Knicks:

“Can be a big key to this team.”

On Drummond replacing Mitchell Robinson by being himself:

“Obviously, Mitch was near and dear to all of our hearts. I think the best part of the situation Andre is in, he’s not coming in to be Mitch. He’s coming in to be himself. So we’ve gotta give him the confidence to go out there and be himself.”

On getting to know Drummond at his birthday party:

“I’ve known him from afar. It’s always been mutual, like hi and bye. Always respect. That was like first time we really got to sit down and have a conversation. It was kind of an icebreaker type of thing.”

On his offseason wrist rehabilitation:

“I just feel like I didn’t do my normal summer stuff. I feel good, but also I know that it wasn’t just my normal summer.”

On how this wrist rehabilitation compared with his previous hand injury:

“It was similar, but I was shooting earlier than I was this time. I was in a cast longer than I was before, when I broke my hand. Plus, [surgery] was a little bit earlier — I think I got surgery right after it happened. I didn’t get surgery until like three weeks later [this time] because I didn’t know it was a necessity.”

On not viewing his disrupted offseason as catching up:

“I don’t want to say I’m catching up. I feel good, but also I know that it wasn’t just my normal summer.”

On the praise from LeBron James and Giannis Antetokounmpo:

“I really do appreciate it. I respect the hell out of them. It’s honestly really cool … I really do appreciate it, and it shows where I’ve grown, but still got a lot of work to do.”

On experiencing the championship summer in New York and finding time to decompress:

“It exceeded expectations, honestly. Winning in New York was no joke. It was a really cool experience. … Have I decompressed at all? Not really. I’m gonna be honest with you, not really. But I’ve had times where I had time to relax. I enjoyed that. I spent time getting away from everything. Most times, it was rehabbing. Once I was out of the cast and cleared, I had obligations I had to go through, so I did all of that. But I feel good. And I know where to go to get to my happy place. I know where to go when I need to decompress. I’m good.”

On what the Knicks can add to the offense after unlocking something during the playoffs:

“I feel like we can do a lot more, do a lot of different things. I think we unlocked something last year in the playoffs at a time of need and it worked. It’s gonna be fun to kind of integrate it from the beginning of the season, too.”

On the Knicks learning they need each other to win:

“I think as a group, we figured out that we need each other to win, obviously, and we need each other to be on the same page. You never know when things are going to turn for you, when things are gonna click for you. But as long as you keep putting the work in every single day, you keep tapping the rock, tapping the rock, eventually it’s going to break.”

On getting to know Rajon Rondo and hosting him at Tarrytown on Tuesday:

“I got to talk to him, got to really get to know him this summer. I definitely watched him. He was just so creative and someone who was innovative in the way they play basketball.

“Definitely an icon when I was younger. So it was really cool to get to know him and his family.”

On Andre Drummond’s rebounding ability:

“One of the best rebounders of our generation.”

On the freedom he felt after winning the championship:

“The ability to celebrate and rejoice and have that joy of a kid without being judged. And also just the freedom of being able to really talk your s— for real, like being able to say you’re the champion and no one being like, well, this or that, whatever.

“It was a much more freeing experience now being an adult and being in that situation than I think I would have ever realized when I was young.”

On how winning the championship differed from how he imagined it when he was younger:

“When you are young, you’re looking at a championship as a sense of accomplishment. I think for me, in that moment winning it, it felt very freeing because a lot of the questions I know people had on me were put to rest.”

On refusing to change himself despite outside criticism:

“I just was never going to change who I was, even when the world was asking me to change who I was, so I could be the character in their story. I just was going to continue to be me.”

On how playing in a smaller market helped his development before arriving in New York:

“We talk about (playing in a) small market as a bad thing. It was a great thing for me because it protected me from having to be a perfect form of myself for the big media markets and stuff. I was able to really grow and hone myself as a person and fine-tune the things that I needed to so when I got (to New York), which wasn’t part of my plan, I was truly the best version of myself.”

On continuing to work rather than complain about criticism or a lack of immediate success:

“I’ve kept my head down and continued to try to be the best human I could be in the world, be the best player I could be even when I needed things to work on. Instead of complaining about why I didn’t get the love or have the immediate success, I just got back in the gym and worked on my game. And this was a year where I finally had enough lessons to really put it together and was given the opportunity to do something special.”

On his mother encouraging him to remain himself:

“My mom always told me to be who I am and never be ashamed to be who I am. To be unapologetically myself even if the love that I love to show people is not reciprocated.”

On mental strength not requiring him to change his personality:

“I think mental fortitude and mental strength doesn’t need to come with a frown on it. You can still smile and have an amazing amount of mental strength and have that Mamba Mentality”

On preparing for the possibility of being traded to Milwaukee midway through last season:

“We were on Zillow looking at Milwaukee. Like, ‘Hey, babe, I went around town, and it’s not that bad. This could be a good spot right here.’”

On embracing whatever role the Knicks needed from him during their championship run:

“Whatever was needed, I was willing to do at the highest level and be a star in my role. I think, in my career, I’ve always talked about my versatility, and it took that word versatility to get this championship.”

On balancing the playoffs with his father’s hospitalization:

“That was at the end of the season, too, and I missed every practice; I missed every shootaround. I only showed up to play the games, and I went right back to the hospital. Shoutout to my team.”

On finding validation through his own approach:

“Is my way the most glamorous way of doing it in the world, especially in the social media world? Absolutely not, because everyone wants instant validation, everyone wants instant gratification. But it is true in the long run, the good guys always win.”

On his championship, family and personal life coming together:

“My skill, my experience and my personal life all came together at the right moment, at the top, top, top of the game. There’s a lot of euphoria in the Towns family right now.”

“A great player. We know he can help us a lot.”

On why joining the Knicks made sense for him:

“I think it just made the most sense in terms of where I’m at in my career, what this team had just done — they had just won a championship — and with the addition of my veteran leadership and what I bring to the table, it just made sense for me to come here. I had a bunch of different options, but this option was the best one for me. I grew up a Knicks fan from young… So it’s a true honor to put this jersey on.”

On taking open 3-pointers without hunting them:

“For me, if the shot is there, I’ll take it. It’s not something I’m hunting. Same thing in Philadelphia. It’s not a shot I’m hunting. If it’s a good shot, I will take it.

“It’s a shot I’ve worked on. Same thing here. I’ve got the green light to do it. If the shot’s open, take the shot. But my main goal is to help the team the best way I can.”

On the skills and durability that have kept him in the NBA:

“[I am] a master at what I do. I’m able to rebound the ball at a high clip. Obviously with the addition of the 3-point shot, being able to be a good pick and roll defender, and just being a great locker room guy overall is what keeps me around.

“I stay healthy. I take care of my body. I do the necessary things to make sure I’m able to play the game at a high level.”

On being the lone newcomer to the Knicks:

“This is the first time I’m the only new guy to a team. So it feels kind of weird. Like an outcast trying to fit in but the guys are very welcoming, they made me feel very welcome to be here.

“Everybody’s been very nice and showing me the ropes of how to be a New York Knick.”

On what he gave Brunson for his birthday:

On getting a head start learning the Knicks’ system:

“I’ve been here [in Tarrytown], just learning their system and how they flow both on offense and defense. So I’ve got a head start on what’s to come.”

On choosing the Knicks in free agency and growing up as a fan:

“This was the best option. Being born in Mount Vernon and then moving to Connecticut very young, I’ve always been a Knicks fan — from Amar’e [Stoudemire] to Patrick Ewing, the list of greats in this organization, it’s a true honor to put the jersey on.”

On Knicks fans taking over Philadelphia during the playoffs:

“It was crazy. It felt like an away game the whole series. They came down and took over the entire arena.

“Crazy seeing some of the fans from [Philadelphia] even wearing Knicks jerseys, too, so the Knicks fanbase is just far and wide. It doesn’t matter where you are in the world. It’s the basketball Mecca, so they did what they were supposed to do.”

On what he still brings as a veteran center:

“I’m able to rebound the ball at a high clip, still. And I’m a very good locker room guy.”

On playing with his finger wrapped for the rest of his career:

“Just so I don’t got to answer this question anymore. There is no other surgery for me to get besides a joint replacement. If I get a joint replacement, I can’t play with it and my career is over. So it will be wrapped until I retire.”

On resolving his past issue with Celtics coach Joe Mazzulla:

“At first, we had a little issue because I’m like, ‘You gotta say sorry for fouling me,’ …But he apologized, and now we’re on the same team, so it’s going to be great, just build together and stuff like that, get to know him as the year goes on. I feel like it’s going to be epic.”

On refusing to criticize the Knicks this season after their championship:

“This year, I will not say a negative word about my New York Knicks. They erased a 53-year drought. They can do no wrong this year to me. They are the reigning, defending NBA champions until further notice, and they will be treated like that on this show by yours truly.”

On what he still expects from the Knicks:

“You gotta make the playoffs. Can’t stink up the joint, gotta make the playoffs now. Can’t be getting bounced out in the first round.”

On not needing LeBron James in New York after the Knicks’ championship:

“We don’t need him in New York. But I’m gonna say something on national television that might shock a lot of people. We know that [LeBron] and I don’t mess with each other. We know that story. If the New York Knicks had lost, I would have come on national TV and begged LeBron James to come to the Knicks. I woulda offered to carry LeBron’s bags. I woulda offered to caddy for him, occasionally, while he’s trying to learn golf.

“But I am not lying, I am not exaggerating, and I am not engaging in hyperbole. If the New York Knicks had lost in the NBA Finals, I would have begged, and I mean begged, LeBron James to come to New York.”

On Karl-Anthony Towns supposedly getting an “unreasonable” offer from the Knicks:

“From what I am told — similarly to what Jalen Brunson did — he is also willing to take a pay cut. But the pay cut that the Knicks are asking him to take, he views as unreasonable.”

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘That’s going to help us, but that can also hurt us’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
Here’s the second Bulletin covering Media Day with everything else that I couldn’t find yesterday.

Apologies in advance for any repeated quotes, but hey, y’all can’t have it all.

Here’s the latest before training camp gets going today, with the first preseason game less than a week away.

On playing through his left wrist injury during the playoffs:

“It was painful. I played through it. I did what I had to do to make sure I was right. I didn’t think I needed surgery. If I had known, I maybe would have got it done sooner.”

On not being satisfied after winning the championship:

“Not being satisfied, I think, is the biggest takeaway moving forward. You still want to figure out how you can grow as a person and as a player. So I will use that experience. As a group, we figured out that we need each other to win, obviously. We need each other to be all on the same page.”

On his confidence in his teammates, with a joke about Josh Hart:

“I have all the confidence in the world in my teammates. Not so sure about Josh Hart; we’ll see how he acts.”

On the confidence and danger that come with being defending champions:

“I think we have the confidence knowing that we did do it. That’s going to help us, but that can also hurt us. So it’s all about how we go into training camp and how we go into these first few weeks to see where we are as a team, and then we’ll be able to adjust or continue to grow.”

On the opening weeks revealing the new Knicks’ identity:

“The first couple of weeks or whatever of the season is going to show us who we are and where we are.”

On wanting to sign an extension with the Knicks:

“I made it known I want to play here. I’ve been a fan since I was young. I would like to get one done, of course. Obviously I would like to get it done so I can feel as comfortable as possible.”

On what it will take for the Knicks to repeat as champions:

“To repeat is gonna take an even higher sense of discipline and execution. And we’re gonna have to be even better than what we showed in the playoffs. All of us are aware that we’re gonna have to bring a whole other level to the table if we expect to have a chance to repeat.”

On the lack of progress on a contract extension and wanting to remain a Knick:

“Are things going to get done? There hasn’t really been much movement or conversation with that, so I don’t think it will get done. But I would love for it to get done. Once the season starts, I’ll probably have that mentality of ‘I don’t really wanna deal with this, I want to try and focus on playing the season.’ I’m sure there will probably be a little extra weight to the jersey. You don’t know the certainty of your situation and obviously it affects home life. There are certain things that you might want to do, but you’re like ‘I can’t, because I have no idea what the situation will be in two months, three months, four months, in a year, if I’m gonna be here or not.’ You don’t know. But hopefully, like I said, I’m a Knick, I’d love to be a Knick and I love the city.”

On the human impact of unresolved contract situations:

“I would hope that that stuff gets done. At the end of the day, we’re humans and I think what sometimes gets lost is that we are people, that we all have lives and things that we have to deal with and fix. I wish I could sit there and say it wouldn’t have any weight or any bearing, but you never know. Some people can handle it great and some people can really struggle with it and that can kill their performance. I hope it gets done, but we’ll see.”

On Jalen Brunson’s “Saturday Night Live” performance:

“I think his performance was fine. I don’t think he has a future in acting.”

On whether Brunson’s $113 million pay cut is still available:

“Is that money still up for grabs?”

On returning to work after the championship summer:

“The weight of the jersey was extremely light this summer. This morning, it was a bit heavier. I think we’re all excited for the opportunity to do it again. We’re not satisfied to just get one.”

On the Knicks’ shot at breaking the no-back-to-back champion trend in the NBA

“We write our own history.”

On the significance of the CBA and second apron in the league’s lack of repeat champions:

“Obviously, it probably shows the significance of the [collective bargaining agreement], the second apron, all those kinds of things. At the end of the day, that’s the past. It has no precedent on what the future is going to hold. For us, we’re not really worried about it. We’re worried about etching our own stories and our own legacies.”

On the Knicks’ hunger to repeat:

“I think we’re all excited for the opportunity to do it again. I think you guys will see that with how we conduct ourselves, with how we play, that we’re not satisfied with getting one and that hungriness that we’re gonna have.”

On the Knicks’ title defense:

“We’ll be hunted, but we’re going to be hunting other teams as well.”

On struggling to sleep after losing the NBA Finals to the Knicks:

“I’ve had a few sleepless nights. It’s been hard to fall asleep sometimes. Hard emotions. But there is a point where you accept that you have to go through it. You have to feel all of it. We don’t want to hide from anything.”

On envisioning finishing his career at Madison Square Garden till the Knicks win it all:

“I had visions of playing in [Madison Square] Garden and finishing my career in the Garden. One of the best places I’ve ever played.

“I was like, ‘Hey, I can’t.’ I couldn’t do it.”

On the Knicks and Jalen Brunson:

“Much respect to the Knicks, obviously. An unbelievable team, unbelievable players. Shout out Jalen Brunson. I love that guy, he’s unbelievable.”
